overview: The Sámi are a continuing Indigenous people with several languages and regional cultures across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. The map’s broad northern outline and 1500 BCE to 800 CE interval do not establish a single ancient kingdom or a fixed ethnic boundary. Early evidence needs careful interpretation; the later examples below show how Sámi households, skills and languages continued to develop.

sections.title: Early evidence, without inventing an ancient kingdom

items.text: At Levänluhta in western Finland, people buried their dead in what was probably a small pond between about 300 and 800 CE. Most of the recovered individuals were women and children. The unusual cemetery raises questions about who was buried there; it does not by itself identify their language.

Researchers connect Levänluhta with Sámi history through earlier genetic work and place names. Food-isotope results show varied diets drawing on land, the sea and fresh water. This is evidence from one Iron Age community south of much of today’s Sámi homeland, not a universal Sámi menu.

The Levänluhta study found that the largest dietary group continued using marine foods after the sixth-century cold period, with a greater marine contribution in some seventh-century burials. Several food sources may have helped people endure environmental shocks. We know the pattern from their remains, not from a surviving shopping list.

Reindeer herding developed gradually and differently across regions. Early Sámi economies combined hunting and fishing with smaller numbers of tame animals, including animals used for transport or as decoys. A familiar modern image of large reindeer herds should not be projected unchanged back into the Bronze Age.

At Brodtkorbneset beside the Pasvik River, seven stone hearths stand in a row; nearby Steintjørna has eight. Radiocarbon evidence places the main occupation between the late eleventh and late thirteenth centuries. Archaeologists interpret the hearths as the centres of neighboring households, probably sheltered by tents.

Food remains at these Pasvik sites include reindeer, whitefish, pike and a little sheep. The animal bones help reconstruct meals and economic choices. Identifying reindeer bones does not automatically tell researchers whether each animal had been hunted or herded.

Brodtkorbneset also produced an iron fishhook, a knife, a hide scraper and a fragmentary comb. Pieces of flint were used with fire-making tools to produce sparks. A place remembered mainly for stone hearths also held work on food, clothing, personal grooming and the daily job of getting a fire started.

In historically documented Kola Sámi siidas, groups separated during spring, summer and autumn to fish, hunt and tend reindeer, then reunited at a winter village. Kinship and shared access to resources linked these households. The year’s social calendar followed useful places as well as changing seasons.

Siida’s Skolt Sámi Heritage House displays a smoke sauna, a storehouse and a root-sewn boat alongside homes. Some buildings reconstruct earlier practices using written and oral evidence. The boat is a reminder that useful building materials included roots as well as timber.

A collection returned to the Sámi Museum Siida in 2024 included a cheese mould from Enontekiö dated 1797 and crossbow stocks reaching back to 1730. Alongside textiles and sledges, such objects preserve practical knowledge. Studying them can help craftspeople recover techniques and pass skills between generations.

In modern Sámi language nests, young children encounter a Sámi language through everyday play and conversation. Adults use that language from the beginning, even when a child initially understands little; children may choose which language they speak. Learning happens while doing things together, not only during a vocabulary lesson.

Writing sample: “Enâmeh láá mii párnááh” means “These lands are our children.” Siida chose this Inari Sámi title from a poem by Matti Morottaja for its renewed exhibition. It is modern, attested community writing, giving an idea about land and responsibility a memorable voice.

A second small sample comes from Northern Sámi: “Movt manná?” means “How are you?” UiT’s university phrase guide prints the expression with its English translation. Northern Sámi and Inari Sámi are distinct languages, so their written forms should not be treated as interchangeable.

ending.text: Sámi people and languages continue beyond the map’s 800 endpoint. Representative institutions, museums and language programs support cultural life today. This record does not describe a people who vanished when an ancient political state fell.
